tips.title: Table, record, field
tips.body: A **table** holds data about one kind of thing. A **record** is one **row** — one student. A **field** is one **column** — one property, such as Name. Get these three right and the rest of the vocabulary follows.

tips.title: Primary key identifies, foreign key links
tips.body: A **primary key** **uniquely identifies** each record in its own table. A **foreign key** is a field that **refers to the primary key of another table**. One identifies, the other connects.

tips.title: Strings need quotes, numbers do not
tips.body: `WHERE YearGroup = 11` takes no quotes because it is a number. `WHERE ClubName = 'Drama'` needs **single quotes** because it is text. Dropping the quotes is the commonest SQL error in the exam.

tips.title: WHERE is not optional on UPDATE or DELETE
tips.body: A `DELETE FROM Student` with **no WHERE** deletes **every record**. Same for `UPDATE`. Always write the WHERE clause, and check it selects only what you intend.

tips.title: Two benefits, and they are different
tips.body: **Redundancy** is storing the same thing **more than once**. **Inconsistency** is what happens when one of those copies is **changed and the others are not**. Redundancy is the cause; inconsistency is the damage.

steps.title: Databases and the words for them
steps.body:
**A database is an organised, persistent collection of data**, structured so that it can be searched and updated efficiently.

**A relational database** stores data in **several linked tables** rather than one big one. The links are what make it relational.

**The six terms the specification names:**

- **Table** — holds data about **one kind of thing**: students, or clubs.
- **Record** — one **row**; all the data about one student.
- **Field** — one **column**; one property, such as `Name`.
- **Data type** — what kind of value a field holds: integer, text, date, Boolean.
- **Primary key** — a field that **uniquely identifies** each record in its table.
- **Foreign key** — a field that **refers to the primary key of another table**, creating the link.

**In the example used through this topic** there are two tables. `Student` has the primary key `StudentID`. `Club` has the primary key `ClubID`. The `ClubID` field **in `Student`** is a **foreign key**: it points at a record in `Club`.

**Why a primary key must be unique** is worth seeing plainly: if two students shared an ID, nothing could tell them apart, and a query asking for "the student with ID 3" would have no single answer.

steps.title: Why split the data into tables
steps.body:
**The specification says a relational database facilitates the elimination of data inconsistency and data redundancy.** Those are two different problems, and the difference is examined.

**Data redundancy** is storing the **same data more than once**.

Suppose there were no `Club` table, and each student record simply held the club's name. There are **5** students, so the club names would be written out **5** times instead of the **3** times needed. The same text is repeated for no reason, wasting space and effort.

**Data inconsistency** is what happens **next**. If the Drama club is renamed, every row holding the old name has to be changed. Miss one — or mistype one as "Dramaa" — and the database now holds **two different answers to the same question**, with nothing to say which is right.

**Splitting the data fixes both.** The name "Drama" is stored **once**, in the `Club` table. Students refer to it by `ClubID`. Renaming the club means changing **one** value in **one** place, and every student automatically follows.

**Note the relationship between the two.** Redundancy is the **cause**; inconsistency is the **damage it eventually does**. Answers that treat them as the same thing lose a mark.

steps.title: Two tables, and changing data
steps.body:
**Querying across two tables** is where the foreign key earns its place. The specification says questions will use **no more than two tables**.

To list who is in the Drama club, the name is in `Club` but the students are in `Student`, so both tables are needed and the **link** must be stated:

```
SELECT Student.Name
FROM Student, Club
WHERE Student.ClubID = Club.ClubID
AND Club.ClubName = 'Drama'
```

The first condition **joins** the tables by matching the foreign key to the primary key. The second filters. Result: **Amara and Elif**.

**Note `Table.Field`** — when two tables are involved, say which table each field belongs to.

**Adding a record:**

```
INSERT INTO Club (ClubID, ClubName)
VALUES (4, 'Debating')
```

**Changing records:**

```
UPDATE Student
SET YearGroup = 12
WHERE YearGroup = 11
```

**Deleting records:**

```
DELETE FROM Student
WHERE StudentID = 4
```

**The WHERE clause is the dangerous part.** `DELETE FROM Student` on its own deletes **every record in the table**. The same applies to `UPDATE`: without a condition, every row is changed. Always write it, and always check what it selects.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Quote text, never numbers.** `WHERE ClubName = 'Drama'` needs **single quotes**; `WHERE YearGroup = 11` must not have them. This is the most frequent SQL error in the exam and it is entirely avoidable.

**Keep the keywords in order.** `SELECT … FROM … WHERE … ORDER BY …`. Writing `WHERE` before `FROM` is not a small slip — the statement is simply invalid.

**State the join condition when using two tables.** `WHERE Student.ClubID = Club.ClubID` is what connects them. Without it every student is paired with every club, and the answer is nonsense. Use `Table.Field` so it is clear which field is which.

**Distinguish redundancy from inconsistency.** Redundancy is storing the same data **more than once**; inconsistency is copies **disagreeing** after one is changed. Redundancy is the **cause**, inconsistency the **damage**. Treating them as synonyms loses a mark that is simply there for the taking.

**Explain a primary key by what breaks without one.** If two records shared an ID, no query could reliably pick out one of them, and any foreign key pointing at that ID would be ambiguous. Uniqueness is not an arbitrary rule — it is what makes the links work.

**Be exact about which table holds the foreign key.** In this example `ClubID` is the **primary key of `Club`** and a **foreign key in `Student`**. The same field name plays two roles, and saying which is which in which table is what a precise answer does.

**Take the WHERE clause on UPDATE and DELETE seriously.** Omitting it changes or deletes **every record**. An answer that mentions this risk when asked about DELETE is showing judgement, not just syntax.

**Only select the fields you need.** `SELECT *` returns everything, which is more data than required and slower. Asking for `Name` alone is better practice, and questions usually name the fields wanted.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **database** is an organised, persistent collection of data.
- A **relational database** stores data in **linked tables**.
- **Table** — one kind of thing. **Record** — one row. **Field** — one column.
- **Data type** — what kind of value a field holds.
- A **primary key uniquely identifies** each record in its table.
- A **foreign key** refers to the **primary key of another table**.
- **Redundancy** is storing the same data **more than once**.
- **Inconsistency** is copies **disagreeing** after a change.
- Redundancy is the **cause**; inconsistency is the **damage**.
- Linked tables store each fact **once**, so a change is made in **one place**.
- Retrieval: `SELECT … FROM … WHERE … ORDER BY … ASC | DESC`.
- **Text needs single quotes**; numbers do not.
- Two tables need a **join condition** matching foreign key to primary key.
- `INSERT INTO table (fields) VALUES (values)` adds a record.
- `UPDATE … SET … WHERE …` and `DELETE FROM … WHERE …` — **without WHERE, every record is affected**.

questions.prompt: Explain what a relational database is, define the terms primary key and foreign key, and explain how using linked tables removes data redundancy and inconsistency.
questions.solution:
A **database** is an organised, persistent collection of data structured so that it can be searched and updated efficiently. A **relational database** stores that data in **several linked tables** rather than in one large one, and the links between the tables are what make it relational.

Each **table** holds data about **one kind of thing** — students, or clubs. A **record** is one **row**, holding all the data about a single student. A **field** is one **column**, holding one property such as `Name`. Each field has a **data type** — integer, text, date or Boolean — which fixes what kind of value it may contain.

A **primary key** is a field that **uniquely identifies each record** in its own table. `StudentID` is the primary key of `Student`. Uniqueness is essential: if two students shared an ID, a request for "the student with ID 3" would have no single answer.

A **foreign key** is a field that **refers to the primary key of another table**. In the `Student` table, `ClubID` is a foreign key pointing at the primary key of `Club`. It is worth being precise here: the same field name is the **primary key in `Club`** and a **foreign key in `Student`**.

**Data redundancy** is storing the **same data more than once**. If there were no `Club` table and each student record simply held the club's name, then with five students the club names would be written out **five** times rather than the **three** actually needed — the same text repeated for no reason, wasting space.

**Data inconsistency** is what that repetition eventually causes. If the Drama club is renamed, every row holding the old name must be changed. Miss one, or mistype it, and the database now holds **two different answers to the same question**, with nothing to indicate which is correct. Redundancy is the **cause**; inconsistency is the **damage**, and they are not two names for the same thing.

**Linked tables remove both.** The name "Drama" is stored **exactly once**, in the `Club` table, and students refer to it through the foreign key `ClubID`. There is no repetition, so there is no redundancy — and because the fact exists in only one place, renaming the club means changing **one value in one row**, with every student record automatically reflecting the change. There are no other copies that could fall out of step.

questions.prompt: Using the Student and Club tables, write SQL to list the names of students in the Chess club, and explain how the query works. Then explain the risks of UPDATE and DELETE statements.
questions.solution:
The student names are in `Student` but the club **name** is in `Club`, so both tables are needed:

```
SELECT Student.Name
FROM Student, Club
WHERE Student.ClubID = Club.ClubID
AND Club.ClubName = 'Chess'
```

This returns **Ben** and **Chloe**.

**How it works, clause by clause.** `SELECT Student.Name` states which **field** is wanted; writing `Student.Name` rather than just `Name` makes clear which table it comes from, which matters once two tables are involved. `FROM Student, Club` names **both tables**.

The first condition, `WHERE Student.ClubID = Club.ClubID`, is the **join**: it matches the **foreign key** in `Student` to the **primary key** in `Club`, so each student is paired only with **their own** club. The second condition, `AND Club.ClubName = 'Chess'`, then filters those pairs down to the club wanted. `Chess` is **text**, so it takes **single quotes**; a number such as `11` would not.

**Leaving out the join condition is the classic error.** The statement is still **valid SQL**, so it runs without complaint — but every student is paired with every club, giving 5 × 3 = **15** meaningless rows. A query that fails loudly is much safer than one that returns a confident wrong answer, which is why the join condition should be checked first.

**The risks of UPDATE and DELETE** come from the same clause. `UPDATE Student SET YearGroup = 12 WHERE YearGroup = 11` moves the three Year 11 students up. Omit the `WHERE` and the statement becomes `UPDATE Student SET YearGroup = 12`, which sets **every student in the school** to Year 12 — including those in Years 9 and 10.

`DELETE` is worse, because the damage cannot be undone by simply running another statement. `DELETE FROM Student WHERE StudentID = 4` removes one record; `DELETE FROM Student` removes **every record in the table**. The table still exists, but it is empty, and the only recovery is from a backup.

The practical safeguard is to run the condition as a `SELECT` first — `SELECT * FROM Student WHERE StudentID = 4` — and confirm it returns exactly the records intended before turning it into a `DELETE` or an `UPDATE`.

examTechnique.body:
Keep the keywords in order — `SELECT … FROM … WHERE … ORDER BY …` — and **quote text but not numbers**. With two tables, always give the **join condition** matching foreign key to primary key, and write `Table.Field`.

Keep **redundancy** (stored twice) apart from **inconsistency** (copies disagree), and never omit `WHERE` from `UPDATE` or `DELETE`.
examinerErrors: Forgetting single quotes around a text value.
Writing the keywords out of order.
Omitting the join condition in a two-table query.
Using redundancy and inconsistency as if they meant the same thing.
Saying a foreign key identifies records in its own table.
Omitting WHERE from an UPDATE or DELETE.
Using SELECT * when the question named the fields wanted.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer quotes **text** and not **numbers**, keeps the keywords in order, and always supplies the **join condition** in a two-table query — knowing that omitting it still **runs** and returns every combination, which is worse than an error. It says which table holds the **foreign key** and which holds the **primary key** it points to, and explains uniqueness by what **breaks** without it. It separates **redundancy** (the cause) from **inconsistency** (the damage), and when writing `DELETE` or `UPDATE` it names the risk of a missing `WHERE` and suggests testing the condition with a `SELECT` first.
